lead: The weekday readings face the mystery of evil and the power of faith. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the lawlessness already at work will be unmasked and destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming, and that those who refuse to love the truth are deceived. In Mark, the day after the cursing of the fig tree, Jesus answers Peter’s astonishment with a call: “Have faith in God”, and promises that prayer offered in faith is heard. Today the Church also keeps the memory of St Ignatius of Loyola and gives two readings for him: Paul’s rule “do everything for the glory of God”, and Jesus’ plain word to the crowds that a disciple must be ready to give up everything, after counting the cost like a builder or a king. The common thread is truth and faith: love the truth, trust God, and do all for his glory.

r.h: Those who refused to love the truth
set: The letter answers a community alarmed by a rumour that “the day of the Lord is already here” (2:2). Paul (the Church receives the letter as his, though some scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name) reminds them of what he had taught: before the Lord’s day there must come a great rebellion and the appearance of “the lawless one” (2:3–4). In today’s verses he says that this power of lawlessness is already at work, held back for now by someone or something he does not name, and that when the Lord comes, he will destroy the lawless one “with the breath of his mouth”.

This is one of the most debated passages in the New Testament. Paul’s readers knew who or what “restrains”, but we do not. Early Christian writers suggested the Roman Empire or the order of law, and others suggested other things; St Augustine honestly confessed that he did not know what Paul meant (City of God 20.19). The main teaching is plain: evil has a limit, Christ will overcome it, and the only protection is love of the truth.
str: vv. 5–7: Paul reminds them of his teaching; the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but is restrained.
v. 8: the lawless one will be revealed, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the manifestation of his coming.
vv. 9–10: his coming is with Satan’s power, false signs and deception for those who are perishing because they refused to love the truth.
vv. 11–12: God lets a powerful delusion work on those who have not believed the truth but took pleasure in unrighteousness.
kw: Opposition to God’s order. The “lawless one” stands for the power that sets himself against God and wants to be worshipped.
what restrains / the one who restrains
A neuter and a masculine form in the same passage. Its meaning is not certain, and the Church has never defined it.
Truth is not only to be believed but to be loved. Those who refuse the love of the truth are open to deception.
vv: For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work
Evil is already present in history. Christians are not surprised by it, nor are they to be afraid.
whom the Lord Jesus will destroy with the breath of his mouth, annihilating him by the manifestation of his coming.
The victory is Christ’s. The language comes from Isaiah 11:4: the word of the Lord is enough.
because they refused to love the truth and so be saved.
Deception is not only the work of a trickster; it grows where people refuse the truth. Love of the truth is a protection.
For this reason God sends them a powerful delusion, leading them to believe what is false
This is a biblical way of speaking of God’s permission: those who persistently reject the truth are left to the consequences of their choice (compare Romans 1:24–28). God is not the author of evil.
ch: The Catechism teaches that before Christ’s second coming the Church must pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers, in which a religious deception offers people an apparent solution to their problems at the price of apostasy from the truth (CCC 675–677). It teaches also that God is never the cause of evil, but permits it, and in his wisdom brings good from it (CCC 311–314). The Church does not try to say who the “lawless one” is, or when he will come, and she warns against calculating the signs; she calls her children to watch and to love the truth.

set: The reading is the second half of a pair. On the way into Jerusalem, Jesus had cursed a fig tree that had leaves but no fruit (11:12–14), then cleansed the Temple (11:15–19). Now, on the way back the next morning, the disciples see that the tree has withered from the roots. Mark places the Temple action between the two parts of the fig tree story, so the tree is a sign: a religion of leaves without fruit stands under judgment. The sign is directed against the failure of those entrusted with the Temple, not against the Jewish people.
Peter points out the tree. Jesus does not explain the sign but turns the disciples to faith in God and the power of prayer.
str: vv. 20–21: the withered fig tree; Peter remembers and points it out.
v. 23: a believer who says to this mountain, be taken up and thrown into the sea, and does not doubt, will see it done.
v. 24: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
kw: Literally “have the faith of God” or “faith in God”. The faith meant is trust in God’s power and faithfulness, not belief in our own power.
Probably the Mount of Olives or the Temple Mount, where Jesus was standing. Moving a mountain was a Jewish figure for doing what seems impossible.
vv: Have faith in God.
The whole teaching is in these words. Everything depends on God, and so everything is possible to one who trusts him.
if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and if you do not doubt in your heart, but believe that what you say will come to pass, it will be done for you.
A bold picture, not an instruction to try magic tricks. It shows the power of faith to overcome what seems immovable, in line with God’s will.
whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
Prayer is not a way to get what we want but a sharing in God’s purposes. St John explains that we receive what we ask “according to his will” (1 John 5:14).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus’ words on faith show that nothing is impossible for the one who believes (CCC 2609–2610), and also that prayer of petition must be made with trust in God’s wisdom, since he knows what we need and his answers are for our true good (CCC 2734–2737). The Church teaches that we should ask in the name of Jesus and with the same mind as his, and then we will be heard. Saints who suffered, such as St Ignatius in his illness and conversion, show that the answer sometimes comes in a form we did not expect.

r.h: Do everything for the glory of God
set: Paul has been discussing whether Christians in Corinth may eat food that was offered to idols (chapters 8–10). His answer: they have freedom, but love for the weak limits it. This passage is his conclusion: do everything for the glory of God, give no offence, and imitate Paul as he imitates Christ. The chapter break falls in the wrong place; 11:1 belongs with the end of chapter 10.
str: v. 31: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all for the glory of God.
vv. 32–33: give no offence to Jews, Greeks or the church of God, as Paul seeks the good of many that they may be saved.
11:1: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
kw: The weight and radiance of God. To live for it is to make God known in daily life.
Paul invites his readers to follow him as he follows Christ. Holiness is learned from living examples.
vv: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.
Nothing is too ordinary. Meals, work and rest can all be offered to God.
not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved.
The measure of freedom is love: not what suits me but what helps others to the Lord.
ch: St Ignatius of Loyola made verse 31 the heart of his spirituality: his motto, Ad majorem Dei gloriam, “for the greater glory of God”, is a way of living this verse. The Catechism teaches that all human activity, however ordinary, can be offered to God and sanctified, so that work becomes a way of holiness (CCC 2427).

r.h: A disciple must give up everything
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem with large crowds, and he turns to tell them what following him means. The language is sharp on purpose: “hate” father and mother, carry the cross, give up all possessions. “Hate” is a Semitic way of saying “love less, put second”, as Matthew 10:37 shows when it says “whoever loves father or mother more than me”. Two short parables, the builder of the tower and the king going to war, show that following Christ demands careful reflection and total commitment, not a casual enthusiasm.
str: vv. 25–27: whoever does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, even life itself, and does not carry the cross, cannot be my disciple.
vv. 28–30: the builder who does not count the cost will be ridiculed.
vv. 31–32: the king who does not weigh his forces makes peace with an approaching enemy.
v. 33: so none of you can be my disciple without giving up all possessions.
kw: A Hebrew idiom of comparison: to put in a second place. It does not mean contempt for family; the commandment to honour father and mother remains.
The verb means to take leave of something, to let go. The disciple lets go of what could keep him from following.
vv: Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
The cross is a daily following, not a single heroic act. Jesus walks the way ahead of us.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost
Jesus asks for clear-eyed commitment. He does not hide the cost, and he does not ask us to carry it alone.
So therefore, none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.
Everything is placed in God’s hands: possessions, plans and ties. What is given to God is not lost but received back in a new way.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544), and that family ties, though important, are not absolute (CCC 2232). St Ignatius, a soldier from the Basque country who was wounded at Pamplona in 1521 and began his conversion while recovering, understood this saying in his own life: he gave up his career and wealth and, after pilgrimage and study, founded with his companions the Society of Jesus, approved in 1540. His prayer in the Spiritual Exercises, “Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty”, is a way of living verse 33.

qa: Who was St Ignatius of Loyola?

Ignatius was born in 1491 in Loyola in the Basque country of Spain and was a soldier. In 1521 a cannonball wounded his leg at Pamplona, and during his long recovery he read the lives of Christ and the saints, which began his conversion. He spent time in prayer at Manresa, where he began to write the Spiritual Exercises, studied in Paris, and with a few companions, among them St Francis Xavier, founded the Society of Jesus, which Pope Paul III approved in 1540. He died in Rome on 31 July 1556. Francis Xavier came to India in 1542 and also worked on the Kerala coast. Ignatius is remembered for his teaching on discerning God’s will and for finding God in all things.
What does Paul mean by “the one who restrains” in 2 Thessalonians?

No one knows for sure. Paul’s first readers knew it, but it is not recorded. Ancient Christian writers suggested the Roman Empire or the order of law; others suggested other things, and Augustine admitted that he did not know. The Church has not defined the meaning. What matters is Paul’s message: evil is limited, Christ will overcome it, and the believer’s task is to love the truth and hold to what Paul taught.
rite: The Syro-Malabar Church remembers St Ignatius with thanks for the Jesuit missionaries and teachers who have served Kerala through the centuries. The Gospel for him asks the question every family can take to prayer: what is my first loyalty, and what would I give up to follow Christ? The Holy Qurbana offers every day the same answer, in which Christ gives himself for us and we offer ourselves to the Father with him.
study: Paul says that evil is limited and that Christ will destroy it. How does this give me courage when I see wrong in the world?
Jesus says, “Have faith in God.” In what situation do I most need to put my whole trust in God?
Ignatius lived for the greater glory of God. What ordinary part of my day can I offer to God’s glory this week?
